name: Alfred Taylor
bio: Marlborough-educated son of a cocoa manufacturer who came into a fortune of £45,000 on coming of age in 1883 and thereafter 'lived a life of pleasure' (his own testimony), keeping perfumed, permanently curtained rooms at 13 Little College Street and later 3 Chapel Street where he introduced young men — the Parkers, Wood, Mavor, Atkins, Scarfe — to one another and to Wilde, who was brought to him by Maurice Schwabe in 1892. Arrested in the Fitzroy Street raid of 12 August 1894 and discharged; arrested again in April 1895, he refused to turn Queen's Evidence against Wilde, was convicted on 21 May 1895 of gross indecency with Charles and William Parker, and was sentenced with Wilde on 25 May to two years' hard labour, Mr Justice Wills declaring it impossible to doubt he had 'kept a kind of male brothel.' The Letters editors give his full name as Alfred Waterhouse Somerset Taylor, born circa 1862, and record that after his release he lived in Canada and the USA.
bio_sources: Taylor's testimony, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 242 (age 33; Marlborough; £45,000; folio '2A2' visible) and p. 286
Mr Justice Wills's sentence, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 339
Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial note, Complete Letters (2000), p. 603 n 2 (born circa 1862; Fitzroy Street raid 12 Aug 1894; refused Queen's Evidence; Canada and the USA)
bio_note: Death date: not found; the trial record carries his sworn age, not a date, and the only 'Alfred Taylor' occurrences in Complete Letters (2000) are pp. 603 and 679n, with no editorial main-particulars footnote carrying dates. The specialist compilations agree the death is unrecorded: Zagria's 'A Gender Variance Who's Who' heads its entry 'Alfred Taylor (1862 - ?) aristocrat, procurer, waiter' and states 'On release Taylor emigrated to the United States where nothing is known of him except that in the 1920s he was working as a waiter in Chicago, for by chance he served Alfred Douglas, Wilde's old lover, who was visiting the city' (zagria.blogspot.com, January 2010, citing Croft-Cooke, Feasting with Panthers (1968), and Ellmann, Oscar Wilde (1988)); a second web page repeats the same Chicago sentence and nothing further. The Wikipedia 'Alfred Taylor (British Army officer)' is Captain Alfred James 'Bulala' Taylor, 1861-1941, tried for war crimes - not Wilde's co-defendant.
